speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Minister of Finance. Would the minister give his opinion on the resolution passed by the British Columbia car dealers, as reported in the Toronto Daily Star of January 22, to refuse to accept any more 1957 model cars from manufacturers until the federal budget, with possible cuts in' the 10 per cent excise tax, is handed down; which situation, if it developed in the rest of Canada, could result in a major tie-up of the Canadian automobile industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: EXCISE TAX
subsubtopic: REPORTED ACTION BY BRITISH COLUMBIA CAR DEALERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would not want what I say to be taken as any indication of any budgetary action that one might have in mind. The motor car dealers of Canada have intimated in each of the past three years that they would like the government to find a way of avoiding the loss which they suffer when the tax is reduced. There have been a great many conversation's between ourselves and the motor car dealers and the manufacturers' association. The last one was the week before last when several alternative methods of dealing with the problem were discussed with the representatives of the motor car dealers. Whether the action taken by the British Columbia branch of the motor car dealers has been taken in ignorance of these discussions or whether it has been taken as a result of the discussions, I do not know at the moment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Has the government, or the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, any plan to provide television service to the Bonaventure and Gaspe areas in eastern Quebec and to the adjoining sections of northern New Brunswick?

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: BONAVENTURE AND GASPE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the policy of the government, pending the report and the recommendations of the royal commission on broadcasting, is unchanged. Under this policy the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been authorized to develop the national television system and to establish television production centres at Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal and Halifax. Also under this policy, licences are granted elsewhere to private applicants with the aim of extending service as widely as possible. If private stations are established in the Bonaventure and Gaspe areas, or in any other adjoining areas, the corporation will provide programs to them by means of television recordings if networks are impractical.
The C.B.C. has submitted proposals to the royal commission to increase the television coverage in areas where private stations are not established. Any such plans will have to be left in abeyance until the commission reports and parliament has a chance to study and act on its recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday, January 18, the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne) asked me whether steps had been taken to expedite the translation into French of committee reports, so as to avoid the six to seven weeks' delay which is said to have occurred in former years.
To answer his question I should first inform him that, as he no doubt knows, the bureau for translations has to carry out the specific duties which are assigned to it by virtue of the legislation under which it was set up. Now those duties consist in providing service to the various departments of the federal government as well as to both houses of parliament. In other words, it has to give such translation services as are required by those federal administrative agencies as well as those required by the House of Commons or the Senate.
With this qualification, I am pleased to inform him, however, that steps have in fact been taken to expedite the translation of committee reports, and that five translators have been added to the personnel of that particular division. I hope, as he does, that as a result of those arrangements the work will be speeded up.

In view of the recent announcement which has been made of President Eisenhower's recommendation to congress of a large appropriation of over $1 million with respect to the Passamaquoddy project, would the government make a statement on Can-
The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston
ada's up-to-date position with respect to this development in New Brunswick?
As the hon. member knows, a joint reference on the Passamaquoddy bay project was submitted by the government of Canada and the United States to the international joint commission on August 2, 1956. Subsequently, the commission set up two boards-an engineering board and a fisheries board- with instructions that they should commence studies and investigations without delay. In order that our sections of the boards could start work immediately, certain moneys were set aside from the allocations made to the Canadian section of the commission for the present fiscal year ending in March 1957.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, January 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. R. F. L. Hanna for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to avail myself, as others have done, of this opportunity to say a few words in this debate. It would be difficult for me to address myself entirely to those subjects which are outlined in the speech from the throne because there is not very much in that speech that is of real importance to most of the people of Canada, and those subjects which are outlined in that speech have been amply dealt with by other members of this party and by other members of the house.
I think the speech itself is probably more noteworthy for the lack of interest it shows

The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston in the common people of Canada than for any other reason. I am surprised, Mr. Speaker, that there was no mention in the speech-no indication whatever-that the people of Canada would receive some relief from the tremendous burden of taxation which they have borne so patiently for so long. There was no mention that they might receive any relief whatever through a lowering of the ever-increasing cost of living, nor was there any suggestion that any assistance will be given to the old age pensioners or to those in receipt of family allowances. I mention these two things together, Mr. Speaker, because it has been quite evident during this debate that most of the Liberal party members in the house have given the impression- whether because this may be election year or not-that there would be an increase in these two items, namely old age pensions and family allowances. If that is so, Mr. Speaker, and if at a later date we find that the government has finally condescended to make an increase with regard to these two items, then I would say to you that that would be one of the most dishonourable things that could occur, because if the government can make, and intends to make, an increase in these two allowances now, then they could have made such an increase last year and the year before. The fact that they have held it up until an election year and deprived these people who are in dire need of assistance of receiving these benefits is, I think, a very despicable thing. There are surely other and more honourable ways the government can employ in order to get votes than the use of this underhanded method, and such bad treatment of a group of deserving people for the sake of party advantage.
Still with reference to the speech from the throne, I notice also that no reference was made to any increased allowances for disabled veterans, for disabled persons or for the blind; the speech from the throne was notorious for these, as well as for a great many other omissions. A moment ago, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned old age pensions and family allowances. They could very well have been increased. It is not my intention at this moment to delve deeper into that question, but I just bring it to the attention of the house to remind members that there is a need, and that Canada can well afford to take care of it, together with other problems which are so pressing today.
It is common knowledge that Canada on a per capita basis is the richest country in the world. We have a national product at present of over $29,800 million which is expected to reach the $30 billion mark and, maybe, pass that. Thus it cannot be said that this

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They bucked them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
-and, as is indicated by one of the members, they bucked them wherever they had the opportunity to do so. One of the other provinces that has made an outstanding record in industrial development is the province of

The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston Quebec. If you asked Premier Duplessis what share the federal government had in that industrialization and that promotion, I am sure he would tell you in no uncertain terms that it was not the federal government that was responsible for it.
Then there is the province of Ontario which is a great industrial province. I must say that probably the federal government has given Ontario more encouragement and more assistance than it has given to all the other provinces put together.
There is one thing, though, Mr. Speaker, for which this government can take credit, and I want to give them full credit for it. It is this. If there is any inflation in this country, they are responsible for it. I am not so sure that there is any real inflation, in the real scientific definition of the word. According to the general interpretation of the word "inflation", it means too much money after too few goods. But with a gross national product of close to $30 billion, I do not think that could be said to be the situation in this instance. When you take into consideration the tremendous amount of credit buying and the tremendous number of people who are continually going into debt in order to get money with which to buy the bare necessities of life, I think it can hardly be said that there is too much money after too few goods.
No, Mr. Speaker; inflation comes from the ever-increasing prices, a situation which is a direct result of the policy of this government. One of the outstanding examples is the announcement made by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) just yesterday when he said he was going to make it easier for those in the middle income brackets to find money with which to build houses by raising the interest rate. How he is going to make it easier is going to be a mystery. Certainly those people who can afford to pay more for the money they get will probably be able to get that money. But the majority of people who are in need of houses are not those people who have incomes of $7,000, $8,000, $10,000 and $15,000 a year. It is those people in the smaller brackets who just cannot afford to pay any higher rate of interest than they have been paying in the past who are going to be affected.
The government's first step in this so-called inflation race was when they set a rate of 3 2 per cent for their short-term treasury bills. That was government policy. Then, of course, the Bank of Canada were forced to set their discount rate at 3| per cent. They had no alternative. That was a direct result of government policy. Then the


chartered banks-and this was another indirect if not direct result of the government's policy-had their cash reserve requirements raised from 8 per cent to a 15 per cent liquid reserve. Then the chartered banks immediately were forced to raise their interest rates and so they have raised them to 6 per cent and 7 per cent and in some cases up to 8 per cent, depending on the security which the individual has.
Under this so-called assistance by the federal government we find that big businesses and people who have money do not find it difficult to get possession of the money which they require. In most of those instances the large oil companies or other similar organizations-I do not pick them out particularly-with their credit behind them and the way they have of putting costs into prices, can afford to get this higher priced money. Hence they are not finding much difficulty. But under the system of this government in permitting interest rates and prices to climb, the little man has a great deal of difficulty in getting the amount of money that he needs in order to carry on his business. The small family firms are indeed finding it difficult and the small farms are finding it difficult. If that is the assistance that the federal government is giving to the little man-and I think it is-to about 75 per cent of the population of this country, I say that it is not too much to be proud of.
Certainly it cannot be said that the wage earner, the white collar earner, is overly prosperous during these times. I think it will be agreed by all hon. members in this house that after the ordinary working man receives his cheque and has paid his monthly accounts he has very little left, that the majority of the people are in the same predicament and that, as a result of this insufficiency of funds with which to carry on, they find themselves so far in debt that they will not get out of it for the next 25 years or 30 years.
I now want to speak for a few minutes about this high cost of living because I think that is one of the places where the government could and should do something. Not only has the price index risen up to the present time but it is continuing its upward trend. I have here an extract from the Western Producer of January 10, which deals in part with this matter. The heading is "Living Costs at New High Despite Food Price Drop". It reads in part as follows:
Although there was a substantial drop in the price of food, the Canadian consumer price index increased fractionally in November to a record 120.4, the third straight month a new high has been reached.
The index is based on 1949 prices equalling 100. In November a year ago the figure was 116.9.

The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston
Then further down the article goes on to say this:
The composite index of Canadian farm products prices at terminal markets declined 2.1 per cent from 212.4 to 208.9. The field products index dropped 0.7 per cent from 165.2 to 164.1, and the animal products index eased from 259.6 to 251.7.
The decline in the farm products index reflected lower prices for both field and animal products. The field products index declined due largely to lower prices for most grains and eastern potatoes. Substantially lower prices for hogs, coupled with lesser decreases for eggs, western steers and eastern cheesemilk, caused the drop in the animal products index.
From that article I think it is clear that the people who are raising these foods are not the ones who are receiving the benefit. While we have prices continually rising, the costs of those things which people need in order to live, namely farm products, are continually going down.
One of the other things which must be brought to the attention of the house, Mr. Speaker, is the tight-money policy of this government. That policy is reflected in the increased debt and credit buying of the nation. Last year the credit buying was the highest since September of 1955 when it reached $342 million.
I should like to quote from a publication of the dominion bureau of statistics, the Canadian Statistical Review. It says here that in the year 1941 the combined cash retail sales and credit retail sales amounted to-I shall read the table, which is as follows:

This shows that the cash retail sales continually declined and the credit retail sales continued to increase. Had it not been for the extended credit buying that has prevailed in this country, this country would have been in a much worse position than it is right now.
I should like, for a moment, to deal with a problem more local in nature, and that is the problem of Banff national park. As everyone in this house knows, Banff national park is the greatest national park in Canada; in fact, it is the greatest national park on the North American continent. It has the greatest population of any national park in Canada. In fact, it has a greater population than all the other parks in western Canada. When we in this house speak of some government assistance to the national parks, we always hear the Minister of Northern Affairs and National
Resources (Mr. Lesage) say the government is spending much more money on the national parks than it ever receives. This might be true. Although the government receives hundreds of thousands of dollars from the two dollar payment for every car that passes through the park gates, that is not the only contribution that the national parks, and particularly Banff, are making towards the progress and prosperity of this country. These tourists who come to Banff national park, or the other national parks in Canada, leave millions and millions of dollars in this country of which every Canadian receives a share. You cannot, therefore, judge the contribution the national park has made merely by saying that so much money was obtained at the park gates.
One of the things I want to bring to the attention of the government, and particularly the minister, is that when improvements are made or buildings constructed in the town of Banff then I believe the people of Banff have every right to have closer co-operation from this government because everything that is done in that park has a personal effect on the people there. I wish to give the government credit for the fact that in the last two or three years there has been much closer cooperation, and particularly in the last two or three months. This is as it should be, and it must continue to improve. If it does not the minister is not only going to hear from the people of Banff, but he will hear from their member in this house as well.
Let me say a word about the new developments that are taking place in Banff and and why it is so necessary that there be closer co-operation in that respect. Within the last few months the government decided to instal a new water and sewage system, or at least to improve the one that is there. There has been a very good water system in Banff and it has been there for years. These people have paid for it through the taxes that were levied. The government suddenly decided, without any consultation with the people of Banff, that they should put in a system which would be large enough to take care of all the tourists that might come to the park, and there are many thousands of them. The cost of this system would be shared, 50 per cent by the federal government and 50 per cent by the people of Banff. This decision was taken without any consultation with the people of Banff, but they are the ones who have to pay 50 per cent of the bills. The people never knew a thing about it until the rates were increased and their 50 % share of the increased rates amount to more than we in Calgary have to pay for equal services.

The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston
I know the minister will say that the government, by contributing 50 per cent, is going tar beyond what is really required. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government should pay at least 75 per cent of that increased cost because the 2,500 people in Banff should not be expected to. carry 50 per cent of the cost of a water and sewage system which will take care of all the tourists who go there for three or four months per year. Lest anyone think I am exaggerating the picture I should like to quote from a letter from the Banff advisory council. Some of the moneys that have been spent in Banff national park are out of all reason; the workmanship is poor and the general construction is not what it should be. I am going to read from a section of this letter from the advisory council to the minister, and I am not doing it behind his back because he knows about it. This letter is dated November 20, 1956. It reads in part as follows:
The council desires to thank you tor your courtesy and for the pains that you have evidently taken to present the department's case from its point of view. They much regret, however, that they are unable to accept, in many cases, the conclusions reached by the department as it seems to them that the facts are not capable of substantiating them.
Then, in another paragraph I find this:
Not having been supplied with any figures which could be checked and verified the council is at a great disadvantage and is not in a position to comment authoritatively on the manner by which the present sewer and water system has been evaluated; but such evaluation would have to take into account the sums expended on installation, repair and maintenance as shown by the department's records, but what the record would not show is the percentage of total cost covering bad workmanship, wasted material and ill-advised lanning. This, of course, extends over a long eriod of time and it would be absurd to attempt any investigation at this late date, but even in the last few years catch basins have been installed at considerable expense and in a short time have been buried under new sidewalks and rendered useless, others have been placed in locations where it was impossible for them to function. Other similar cases of waste of public funds could be cited. Such expense appears on the records, but there is nothing to show the disparity between actual cost and what the work should have cost had it been performed in a workmanlike manner.
Then, the concluding paragraph reads as follows:
Under these circumstances, therefore, the council feels that it cannot approve either of the new schedule of rates or of the manner in which it was put into effect. They also strongly urge that, in the future, no changes in tax or licence schedules be made without opportunity being afforded the parks residents, through their representatives, to investigate them and discuss them with the department and further that all major projects of construction or maintenance shall be open for competitive tender and that the citizens shall have the right to appoint a qualified inspector with authority to insure the carrying out of any project in a workmanlike and satisfactory manner.

The council feels that if the residents of the parks are to pay for all improvements they have the right to demand that they shall be consulted before such improvements are undertaken and to specify the manner in which they shall be done.
I point that out to show you that, to a large extent, federal government expenditures in national parks have been wasted. The projects have not been completed in a workmanlike manner and there has been a lack of planning. I say to the minister, therefore, that when things are being done in Banff national park the people, through their advisory council, should be fully consulted. These contracts should be let by tender and not be carried on by patronage.
I have not very much time left and I should have liked to deal extensively with the question of agriculture. However, my time has passed so rapidly that I will not have much opportunity to do that. Nevertheless, I wish to say that this is one of the great industries in western Canada, and in other parts of Canada as well, that has been neglected by this government. The ever increasing costs of agricultural production have made it almost impossible for them to stay out of debt; in fact, it has not been able to keep them out of debt. We as Social Crediters are firmly convinced that agricultural prices should be based on parity, and that there should be some recognition of this by the federal government in the policies which they pursue in order that the farmers of western Canada will be given some fair share of the national income.
When we consider the prices which farmers get for the goods they sell as compared with the goods which they are forced to buy we find that at the end of the calendar year, or their fiscal year, they have very little left to carry on. I would like to recommend to the government one of the things mentioned in the Gordon royal commission report, namely, that the government consider this session giving farmers cash payments for wheat stored on the farm. I know the royal commission suggested that cash payments should be given to the farmers for wheat stored on the farm in relation to the quota, but I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that that is not good enough. Farmers should be given more than a cash payment within the quota limit. They should be given cash payments sufficient to ensure that they will have moneys to carry on during the year or at least enough to keep them out of their ever-increasing debt.
I can only say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the consensus in this house, certainly of farm members, is borne out in the message given on January 4 by Mr. A. T. Baker

in a broadcast on behalf of the Alberta Wheat Pool. This is what he said in part:
It is a serious matter, however, that we in agriculture find ourselves in a state of semidepression while nearly all other sections of the nation are enjoying record prosperity. With clear heads and common sense we must seek a solution to the problem of our unfortunate relegation to the bottom of the economic structure.
It seems to me that short paragraph of Mr. Baker's address pretty well sums up the position in which western agriculture finds itself.
I would like to deal at great length with the agricultural problem. I have my notes before me but the time has slipped away. I can assure you though that when this question comes before the house again we shall have something to say about it. There are other problems too that are of major importance in my constituency. The declining of the coal industry is one of them. The question of labour is another. There are many more that I should like to deal with at greater length than I have found it possible to do in the short time that is available to me on this occasion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I through you, sir, extend to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne my warmest congratulations on the very excellent manner in which they discharged their duties. My congratulations at this time are all the more sincere because I recall that about 10 years ago I had the honour of moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I wish at this time to congratulate the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Kickham) on the excellent speech he made yesterday. The fact that he made that speech, talked about and discussed many of the important problems that affect Prince Edward Island at this time, makes it unnecessary for me to talk at any great length now.
There is one matter, however, that is causing our farmers, more particularly our potato farmers, much concern at this time, namely, the unfair tariff arrangements on potatoes that exist at the present time between Canada and the United States. About two years ago I spoke on this problem in this house. At that time I advanced reasons why I thought this unjust tariff should be renegotiated. I do not intend to put on the record now any of the arguments I used then. I understand, however, that an application has been made to GATT for permission to renegotiate the tariff agreement between Canada and the United States and that such permission has been granted. I hope that the tariff experts of Canada and the United States, if they have
The Address-Mr. MacNaught not already done so, will soon get together and try to work out a more equitable tariff arrangement on potatoes.
I intend now to discuss for a few moments the preliminary report of the Gordon commission on Canada's economic prospects, more particularly as it applies to the mari-times. It is unfortunate, I think, that this report has received such unfavourable press reports, particularly in the maritime newspapers. These reports seem to deal with the negative aspects of the report and ignore all the good suggestions that the report contains. I think the report must be considered as a whole and not have parts picked out of context and commented on. In my opinion, the report contains much that is good and much that will be of lasting benefit to the maritimes if carried out with the utmost co-operation of all parties concerned.
The most important problem of the maritimes is that of transportation, the problem of getting products of the farm and the sea to market. I am glad, therefore, that the commission has devoted a substantial part of its report to the problem of transportation.
The report says in paragraph 8 at page 101:
It seems evident that the transportation facilities of the Atlantic region are in need of improvement but it was not possible for us to undertake the kind of detailed study of the problem necessary in order to make positive proposals about the most appropriate measures which should be taken in order to provide solutions.
I doubt, Mr. Speaker, whether any brief presented to any economic commission during the last 50 years from persons in the maritime provinces has not contained some reference to transportation. It is our most important problem.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And the government has done nothing about it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries

speechtext: The commission therefore recommends-and I agree very much with this recommendation-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And the government has done nothing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries

The commission suggests that this should be the subject of a special inquiry which should also include in its terms of reference a re-examination of the present effects of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. The Maritime Freight Rates Act was passed in 1927, I think, and has had a very beneficial result on the economy of the maritime provinces since that time. Many of the good and beneficial effects of the act, however, have been nullified or whittled away by the horizontal increases that have taken place in freight rates during the last 10 years. I was most pleased, therefore, to

The Address-Mr. Rowe see this recommendation in the report. It is one of the recommendations that the commission suggests should be carried out as soon as possible. I therefore urge the government to lose no time in appointing a commission to look into our transportation problems and more particularly the effects the horizontal increases in freight rates have had on the beneficial effects of the Maritime Freight Rates Act during the last ten years.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to comment on the speech from the throne I feel I must add my congratulations to those which have been extended to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on the able manner in which they discharged their respective duties. Although there has been a wide discussion on the speech from the throne in the limited number of days that we have been given to deal with it, there is not very much to discuss in the speech from the throne. It appears to be somewhat of a pre-election document filled with empty generalities and probably preceding the bringing down of a handout budget before voting day next June, which will in all likelihood be arranged so that we will have even less time to discuss the budget than we have had to discuss the speech from the throne.
I am sure that a great many people throughout the country have been disappointed by the contents of the throne speech. There is very little mention in it of the real problems which confront the people. Farmers throughout the country are disturbed. They find themselves in a steadily declining position and have become the most marginal group in Canada. In comparison with other industries those engaged in agriculture justifiably feel they are forgotten people. The costs of production have been steadily increasing and no other industry in Canada has a smaller margin of profit before taxes. In fact, other industries have almost double what the farmers have by way of return before income taxes. This does not seem to concern the government although it concerns almost everyone else in Canada. The government seems to be following its normal course of smug complacency. In fact, hon. members on the government side of the house do not seem to be very interested in the speech from the throne; very few of the ministers have spoken on it and very few of them even bother to remain in the house to listen to the comments of those who do wish to enter into this debate. The members of the government have been in power for so long a time that they have

grown satisfied with themselves and nothing seems to matter to them as long as it does not involve them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: See them smiling even now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Governments are like machines and when they have been in power for a long time they wear out and become obsolete.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Some wear out faster than others.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That comment came from one of the younger members, who has less experience in the cabinet; but he has only to look at his colleagues and examine their tired appearance in order to realize that this government is wearing out.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Your government wore out in about six weeks.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Liberal government is indeed worn out. Indeed if democracy is to survive we must have alternative governments. Never was Canada more in need of an alternative government than she is at the present time. This government has been in power for so long that the people of Canada are becoming alarmed at its attitude. It is no mere figure of speech to say that the complacency of this government is now recognized by everyone. They would surely even admit that political expediency has been their watchword down through the years.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They are getting pretty rusty.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No government with such a vast majority can remain in power for a long period of time without growing, as they have grown, arrogant and contemptuous of parliament itself, showing utter disregard of questions of importance that are directed to them, and they are applauded by a host of followers. And they never receive more applause than when they give the emptiest and smartest answers in order to curtail interruptions. In fact, only the other day one hon. member said that the members on that side of the house were being criticized and indeed even the cabinet ministers were being condemned. Apparently it is a serious thing to members of the Liberal government when cabinet ministers are criticized by members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How terrible!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

The view is that these men have been in power for so long that they should not be attacked and nothing should be said that would show disrespect toward them. Indeed, it is not just a case of showing disrespect; it is a matter of casting doubt concerning their type of intelligence. We have

The Minister of Trade and Commerce tells us that even if we are buying to an extent of well over a billion dollars more than we are selling to the United States, that is a sort of prosperity. It is true that in the meantime the prices of these articles have increased, like the

close to $1 billion more than they need. Then the government wonders why our farmers and our labour men are dissatisfied; why the people who have not benefited from all this are asking whether they can afford to keep their child at a university.

Where are we going, Mr. Speaker, so far as the commonwealth is concerned? What is our policy? Can the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) tell us? No, he cannot tell us.

speechtext: But when the chips are down, as the saying goes, when their leaders are almost crippled under the burden of responsibility, when the nation that has been the beacon light of hope and security down through the centuries, the nation that took the lead in 1914, the nation that took the lead in 1939, the nation that was almost brought to her knees before our great friends to the south entered those wars, when that nation is in trouble, when its leaders are struggling for support, what do we do?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We sold them out.

The little nation of Australia, not nearly as large as Canada, was not consulted, was not so proud that they had to be consulted first. Oh no. But our Secretary of State for External Affairs, much as he loves the old land and praises it with honeyed words, could not stand with them because he thought he should have been consulted. Now he supports the United States of America which says that it does not want to be consulted. He opposed Britain for going into the Suez and he supports the United States of America when the government of that country asks congress: Now that we have got Britain kicked out, can we go in?
He opposed Britain because Britain said that, if allowed to do so, it would stay there until there were signs of peace and the dangers of war in that area were eliminated. He opposes them for taking that stand. Yet he supports the United States of America when its government asks permission from congress to go in there but says it will not go in until Nasser asks them to come. Britain and France told the United States of America that Russia was sending technical advisers, weapons and machinery to support the Arab countries which had threatened to eliminate Israel but even so the United States said: You must get out. Now the United States wants to go in there but is not going to go in without permission even though the whole road from Bulgaria to the North sea is plugged with Russian troops and equipment.

Do these facts not shock or shake this government?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Do the members of the government think that because they talk the most and travel the most of any cabinet ministers since confederation they know everything about the whole world? Never had we had such talkers and travellers as we have in the present government. They travel around the world. I do not mind the expense, Mr. Speaker. I have had travelling expenses that I paid myself and I know what they amounted to. The taxpayers of Canada are so accustomed to paying high taxes and watching reckless expenditure that even the money spent by these travelling cabinet ministers does not seem to disturb them. In fact, some of the farmers in my district would have spent more if they had had the opportunity.
But, Mr. Speaker, where do we stand? Where are we headed? Is the commonwealth worth anything or not?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You would not think so, to hear them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Are we supposed to be a partner in the commonwealth? Do we pose in election campaigns and at Lions club meetings as the senior partner? Do we shove our chests out and say we are the brightest gem in Her Majesty's crown? Are we that great? Then, boys, England expects every man to do his duty. The commonwealth expects that the senior partner will be the senior partner in trial as well as in triumph. Where are we headed? There is no question that we are either in the commonwealth or we are not in it. If we are not in it, we will depend on the dollar sign and the dollar bloc or we will have to depend on communism and the Soviet bloc.
Do not sell the commonwealth short. I know there are those in the government who will applaud. I know there are those who are from the old land. I know there are those from every country in the world who are being assimilated in Canada and who realize that the British commonwealth of nations is the greatest assembly, the greatest partnership, the world has ever known. Whether they are Ukrainians, Czechoslovakians, Austrians, Poles, Netherlanders, no matter from where they have come, they are here because of the British commonwealth of nations.
There is no greater Liberal fetish, no greater Liberal delusion than the delusion of those who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker, in pretending that we who sit to your left are clinging to the old strings of colonialism,


that the British commonwealth is only for the sheltered few and that they are the champions of Canada's present status. A quarter of a century ago, Mr. Speaker, I heard in this parliament some of the members on that side bragging that they had won this status for Canada. Yes, I heard the late minister of justice and the late prime minister boasting that they had won it. You would have thought to hear them on the hustings that the only status Canada had was a status with a Liberal tag on it.
Who won this status for Canada? Who won our independence? We are grown up. As has been said in years gone by, certainly we are daughters in our mother's house but we have been mistress in our own for a long time. Canada is an independent country. She was not made independent within the British commonwealth. Her independence made her allegiance to the old land that much stronger.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, you know very well, as do many other hon. members on all sides of this house who served in the first great war, that this status was won for Canada from 1914 to 1918, when 60,000 Canadians paid the price. When the late Sir Robert Borden signed the treaty of Versailles, Canada signed as an independent nation. Her status was not won in 1926 at the conference attended by the Liberal statesman of that day. Her status was won between 1914 and 1918. When Sir Robert Borden signed that treaty of Versailles he said in this parliament that the tears rolled down his cheeks because as he signed the treaty for Canada as an independent nation he felt he was signing it with the blood of those who slept in Flanders fields rather than with the ink that was used a few years ago by Liberal politicians.
Mr. Speaker, we have a part to play and we have a responsibility. Again I say this: Do not let anyone sell this great institution short. The Canadian people will not allow any government to forfeit the great chance we have to become still greater in the British commonwealth of nations. Ever since I was a small boy I have heard it said that the sun never sets on the British empire, that it comprises one-quarter of the world. I just checked up here recently and found out the facts. Despite those facts there are those who sit back and say it is too bad, but the old land is through; that the commonwealth has lost her place in the sun; that we now will look north or south. Those sitting on the government benches have allowed over the last 20 years another dangerous trend to develop, so that about 70 per cent of our business is now done with the United States of America.

Stop and think of the matter. Never in the history of human relations and trade relations has any nation gambled as Canada has done. No other nation in the world has ever put so many of her trade eggs in the one basket. Yet, Mr. Speaker, some of the grandfathers and fathers of those young hecklers across the floor to your right, in the years gone by fought an election to have commercial union with the United States of America, and again in 1911. In 1925 I remember so well what happened. The Minister of Finance-he is not in the house; he is still in Montreal-some years ago said, "We do not believe in a brick for brick policy with the United States. We believe in countervailing duties. We will raise our tariffs when the United States raise their tariffs. We will have a countervailing system". In other words we will send our fiscal responsibilities and prerogatives down to Washington and will do what they do. Then a few years later the leader said, "We should like to raise tariffs against the United States of America with this trade coming in as it is, but we must not provoke the United States".
He said we must not provoke them. It would be too bad to provoke them. Mr. Speaker, since before you and I were born, every year consistently we have sold more to the old land, than we have bought from her. I spoke about the British commonwealth covering 25 per cent of the world area. She has more than that percentage of the world trade. Twenty-seven per cent of all exports of the free world today are coming from the British commonwealth of nations. Thirty-one per cent of all the imports are used by the British commonwealth of nations. This government are turning their eyes to Washington, afraid to provoke them, saying where they lead we will follow, even though they are condemning Britain for the same course, condemning Britain on the left hand and following the United States in an even more radical course on the right hand. Mr. Speaker, it is a spectacle that would be a comedy if it was not bordering on a national tragedy.
Mr. Speaker, what we should be doing and what our statesmen should be doing is this. I have no criticism for them at all for travelling; in fact for all they do at home they might as well be travelling. I would rather see the Minister of National Health and Welfare travelling, whether he is talking to bewhiskered men in Ceylon or wherever it might be. I am proud to see him travelling and gaining knowledge of world affairs.
But, Mr. Speaker, I say that we should not sell this commonwealth short. Instead of looking to Washington we should be giving study to our part in the British commonwealth
The Address-Mr. Rowe of nations, and how we can unite with western Europe. The hope of civilization rests more with the British commonwealth of nations united with western Europe than it does with the United Nations organization that can be defeated by those it is trying to control. Western Europe and the commonwealth combined, despite what some people think about the sterling bloc, today control 59 per cent of all the exports of the world and 65 per cent of all the imports. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is very glib with interruptions. If these figures startle him, let him deny them. If he were in his place he would probably say they cannot be true. Did the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration question them?

speechtext: I did.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am not here to educate the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. He has been around here for a long time, and he should have learned more.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext:
The United Kingdom herself has given us a favourable trade balance down through the years. Britain imports 70 per cent of all she buys from western Europe and the commonwealth. She is playing her part as a partner. I think it is high time we played our part as a senior partner. My leader has asked repeatedly for a commonwealth conference. Before he became leader of this party he asked for one, and he has done so since. One of the first things he did when he became leader was to urge that we should have a British commonwealth conference. We have pleaded with this government for one. The answer has been no. The Prime Minister has said it is not convenient for him now. The ex-prime minister of the United Kingdom has gone out of public life perhaps for good, broken physically and almost broken-hearted. But no; we have no time for a conference. The new leader has come into office facing an economic crisis. The nation has been brought almost to her knees economically. On the floor of the House of Commons pleas have been made that the commonwealth nations should get together; that we should have a restudy of the matter; that we should bring this subject of international trade before the conference and find out, after careful study of this allimportant subject, where we stand and what we might do.
I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, and neither are you, whether, when we are confronted with a situation such as this we can arrange to change the picture overnight. But before I resume my seat I say in all sincerity that

The Address-Mr. Martin
we as a senior member of the commonwealth, independent of party, race or creed, should be ashamed to sit idly by and see develop a situation and a trend that threaten the economic soundness of the greatest institution, the greatest organization, the greatest and most successful experiment in human relations that world history has ever recorded, one that has shaped the pattern of the United Nations. The failure of the United Nations to follow that pattern has been responsible for its greatest lack of success.
Mr. Speaker, if this government are so sure of returning to power I urge upon them that, if they are interested in the generations that are yet to come, they have some research undertaken but not by a Gordon commission. Do not pick somebody whom you are going to make a cabinet minister to tell you how to win the next election by telling people that by 1980 they will be so happy that they will not have to work at all, that they will eat more, drink more and have more fun.
We do not need that in Canada. We want someone who will look into this and find out if Canada is a senior partner of the British commonwealth, and if she is playing her part as such. I do not like to think, Mr. Speaker, that our people have to go to the United States for jobs fabricating our raw resources to be sold back to us. I do not like to depend on the whims of Washington. I do not like to have our international affairs guided by our glib-tongued twin travellers in external affairs who follow the United States of America. I would rather that even when they have a little doubt they would follow the motherland that has given leadership to the world down through the years and, Mr. Speaker, could give even stronger leadership in the future if she were supported by her partners. Combined with her partners she can still be the greatest nation in the world; separated from them she will fall apart, and then we will have to line up either with the Yankee dollar or Soviet dictatorship.

I thought most of the people in this country supported those who spoke for this nation at San Francisco in 1945, when we affixed our signature to the charter of the United Nations and joined with Great Britain and the United States and other freedom-loving nations of the world in seeking by that instrument to set up for the second time in 25 years an organization by which we hoped to minimize the occasions of war and provide for our world some semblance of tranquility in order.
The signature of the prime minister of Canada was attached to the charter of the United Nations in the presence of representatives of the opposition. I well remember the late Mr. Gordon Graydon's views, and he was present at the signing of the charter in San Francisco. He was one of the staunchest friends of the United Nations and strongly supported the obligations that flowed from our signature to its charter. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre will remember that at the preparatory commission of the United Nations in the fall of 1945 Mr. Gray don spoke about the value of the United Nations as it was then understood in Canada.
The view he gave then is still the view of this government and I believe of the majority in this house and in this country. There was no suggestion by him, nor is there any suggestion now by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that the United Nations is a perfect organization, that it has so developed its processes of adjudication and conciliation or that its constitution is such that it is capable of dealing finally and effectively with every problem in international life today. What Mr. Graydon said and what we say now, as the President of the United States said yesterday and as Mr. Harold Macmillan, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom said a year ago in the United Nations, is that this organization

with all its faults and with all the frustrations that have attended its operations in 10 years, represents for all of us in the long term the best hope for mankind.
The fact that it has not been possible to implement article 43 and give it, as an hon. member suggested yesterday, the kind of sanction necessary to make its legislative effort effective is not because of any fault of Canada, nor is it the fault of the United States or of the United Kingdom. If the United Nations has not yet achieved the powers involved in the kind of sanction that would make this organization fully effective, for example, in the case of Hungary, the fault lies at the doorstep not of any country in the free world but of the Soviet union, which has consistently refused to give effect to the implications of article 43. To say that the United Nations is one of the cornerstones of our foreign policy is not to suggest that we believe it to be a perfect instrument or organization; it is certainly no justification for the view that we have abandoned the North Atlantic Treaty Organization or that we have abandoned reliance on the potential and actual value of the commonwealth of nations.
Mr. Churchill, as prime minister of the United Kingdom, had much to do with the setting up of the United Nations. He and Mr. Roosevelt and Mr. Mackenzie King, among others, played a great part in the inception of that organization and no one would suggest that because Mr. Churchill had been disposed to act as he did he was anxious to see the liquidation of the empire in which he found so much to be admired. To suggest that we have abandoned our other obligations in the commonwealth or under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization is to suggest something that is simply not in harmony with the facts. Mr. Speaker, in the closing minutes of what is probably the last debate on the speech from the throne in this parliament, I intend to speak about the economic condition of the people in the area of that part of Canada which I have the honour to represent.
Today many of the producers in that part of Canada are bankrupt, and the people in the communities and cities are facing an economic slump. I wish to discuss this matter very briefly, and to close in time to give the government an opportunity to reply to an amendment I propose to move at the close of my remarks.
The cause of the economic conditions in that part of Canada is the extent to which the cost of living has been allowed to rise in recent years, seriously affecting the producers' operating costs. Each year costs of operation of the agricultural producers have spiralled until today, with decreasing returns, they are facing bankruptcy, as I have said. Every other business in Canada affected by increasing costs of operation merely passes on those increased costs in the form of increased prices to the consumer.
The Liberal government is solely responsible for the present spiral in the cost of living. I well recall when in the years following world war II the government proposed to lift price controls. We pleaded with them to leave the controls in force. We told them that if they took off price controls costs of living and costs of operation would spiral, and we would have an inflationary result in Canada that would ultimately bring about the ruination of the country. They replied, "Oh, well, there is nothing to fear; there may be a few increases in the cost of living, but the law of supply and demand will soon

The Address-Mr. Castleden
operate and competition will come into play in such a way as to level off everything".
There has been no levelling off. The cost of living and the cost of operating have continued to increase year by year over the past 10 years. Either there is no competition, or the so-called law of supply and demand is not operating.
What I wish to emphasize, however, is that in Canada there is one industry which cannot pass on Its increased costs of production to the consumer, and that industry is agriculture. No business can long continue to operate when its costs of operation are greater than the returns to the industry. In support of what I have said I am going to quote the words of the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool when he recently referred to the condition of the farmers in the prairie area. At that time he said:
The price he received for his grain and other agricultural products was too low to keep the average farmer out of debt. . . . The result is that many farmers are dipping into reserves to keep going while other farmers are accumulating debts which will be extremely difficult to pay at present prices.
Here is the ominous part of the whole situation. What of the future? Nothing has been done, nothing is being done to prevent the cost spiral from continuing. He went on to point out:
The disparity between costs and prices will in all probability continue to have a serious effect on farm people throughout the coming year.
It is because of the emergency facing these farmers that I rise at this time to protest the existing situation and the do nothing policy of the present government. In fact it is even worse than that. As evidence of what is happening, may I say that young, efficient farmers by the hundreds are selling out and leaving the farms even in the very constituency of the Minister of Agriculture, who was sent here 20 years ago to take care of agriculture and look after that industry for Canada. A more deliberate ruination of agriculture can scarcely be imagined.
Since the government are responsible for this condition, one would have thought that at least they would have introduced some measures to alleviate the situation. At least a parity price program could have been introduced which would have maintained a proper relationship between the selling prices of the farmers' goods and their income on the one hand and their costs on the other. Then the farmer could survive. But the government has left the farmer to the mercies of a cost-price squeeze.
Agriculture is one industry which cannot control its sales or prices, and a parity price program is imperative if agriculture is to

survive. The Liberal government and private Liberal members from Saskatchewan as well as the other prairie provinces, have always voted against a parity price program, and the prairie farmer is being left in a bankrupt state. Last year when cash advances were needed Liberal members voted against them. The government has failed to provide interior government storage for surplus grain in order to prevent spoilage, permit farm deliveries and give relief to the producers. The government has refused to do anything.
What contribution has the Minister of Agriculture made? In the face of the present deplorable condition of agriculture, for which he is responsible as minister, he continues to give the impression in the east and the west that farmers in the prairie areas are well off, in spite of every evidence to the contrary; and the minister knows it. He has not only failed to protect agriculture but has left agriculture open to the dangers of inflation. This misrepresentation of the actual conditions of the farmers of the west can only be described as one of the greatest betrayals of agriculture the history of Canada has ever known.
Millions of bushels of grain are wasting on the prairies. Millions of bushels of grain are piled in heaps or in bins open to the weather. If storage had been provided when the surplus accumulated this waste could have been prevented. This is the situation we have at a time when a billion people in Asia and Africa are hungry, people whose good will we need so badly. If the government had spent one-tenth of what it has spent on armaments, many of which are obsolete, on the feeding of these people and the promotion of peace we could have relieved the situation of the farmers and helped agriculture. The government continues to spend almost $2 billion a year on armaments and less than one-tenth of that amount in trying to promote peace and create good will.
In view of the fact that agriculture must have parity prices I move, seconded by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell), the following amendment:
That the motion be amended by adding the following words to the said address:
"We regret, however, that Your Excellency's advisers seem to favour a flexible price support program, the effect of which is to leave the agricultural industry in a state of uncertainty and insecurity; we also regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to take the necessary steps to establish a system of parity prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure 100 per cent parity of income for agricultural producers.''

Mr. Speaker, I rise on this occasion to speak very briefly on two or three matters that are of paramount interest to myself, to the people

One of my reasons for speaking at this time is to pay tribute to my friend the late Mr. Ross, former member for Hamilton East.
I know that when parliament assembled last November the usual eulogies were expressed, but I do wish to pay my respects on behalf of the people of his constituency and of Hamilton. Mr. Ross was one of those persons who very seldom spoke in the house, but our people back home appreciated a quality in him which was much more important, that of getting things done. I wish he could have been here yesterday when the estimates were tabled to see the results of some of his endeavours. I wish to thank the Minister of Public Works and the government for their understanding of our problems in Hamilton and their confidence in the future of our expanding city.
This year, according to the 1957-58 estimates just tabled, the Department of Public Works will be spending $1,700,000 for harbour improvements and developments. These expenditures have been brought about to a great degree by the tenacity with which the late Mr. Ross represented Hamilton East. For the information of hon. members I might also add that while this large amount is to be spent in Hamilton, the benefits will be felt throughout the surrounding area over the next few years. Hamilton is the hub of shipping for this area. We rank third in all Canada for tonnage shipped. It is the hub for such cities as Niagara Falls, St. Catharines, Guelph and so on. Once again, as I have said, we have broken the tonnage record for Hamilton.
I now wish to say just a word about another matter of great importance. Many members of this house have spoken about an increase in pension for the old age pensioner. I have subscribed to this measure from the day I first arrived here, and I am pleased that this worth-while cause has caught fire. This is a problem of interest to everyone. We all expect to be senior citizens some day. The welfare of our senior citizens is everyone's business. Life expectancy is increasing, so it is becoming more and more necessary that greater attention be paid to this group. I believe an increase at this time will greatly enhance the opportunity for full employment, in which the government has always been interested. It will put more money in circulation, will cause
The Address-Mr. Reinke more goods to be consumed in Canada, and will contribute toward a more orderly distribution.
I do not believe that by increasing the old age pension any incentive to thrift or economy will be lost. On the contrary, every dollar paid to old age pensioners will be spent on goods and services, and will help create a better standard of living for others. It is indeed demoralizing in our economic and social system to have one group of people live under stringent circumstances. I realize, of course, that an increase in the old age pension will present a problem to our government. According to our estimates, just tabled, family allowance payments in 1957-58 will amount to $412,265,000; old age security payments for 1957-58 will amount to $392,536,000, making nearly $805 million for these two important items alone.
An increase of $20 per month would bring our expenditure for old age security to nearly $600 million, or the two combined to nearly $1 billion, almost 20 per cent of our total budget. But I believe most Canadian citizens are anxious to pay for these allowances, and when I say "most" I include persons in both high and low income brackets. I have not had one complaint about the 2 per cent deduction added to personal income tax for this purpose, and if necessary I am sure the average person would gladly pay 3 per cent to give our older folks a better life.
I feel, however, that some of our provinces have been rather shoddy in their approach to this problem of assistance to our aged. I believe that people today are expecting more in the way of security, and are prepared and anxious to pay for it. In an article appearing in the Ottawa Journal of yesterday I notice that reference is made to the new tax-free pensions in Germany. I have not time to read the article now, but just briefly it indicates that under present economic conditions there, a man retiring after 40 years of work would get a tax-free pension of up to $110 a month, the equivalent in purchasing power of about $220 here. The amount would increase in the case of inflation. The opposition socialists say the plan does not go far enough. Of course I suppose socialists, like our friends opposite, are the same anywhere in the world. It seems to me that this is a comprehensive type of plan and one which we probably could not extend that far.
On a former occasion, Mr. Speaker, I spoke rather elaborately about the national health insurance plan. I do not propose to deal with that matter at this time, except to say that in view of the generous proposal made by this government for a plan which will cover

The Address-Division all Canadians I think it is a shame that at least one of the two larger provinces does not accept the proposal. I hope the people of Canada, and particularly those in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, realize that without this acceptance by one or the other of these largest provinces we cannot have a majority of Canadians participating, and the rest of Canada is to suffer as a result.

subtopic: SUEZ CRISIS-EGYPTIAN REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING EMERGENCY FORCE
SUEZ CRISIS-EGYPTIAN REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
Does the Canadian government have any information to the effect that, during the Suez crisis last fall, the prime minister of Egypt, or someone on
his behalf or on behalf of his government, made representations through diplomatic channels or otherwise, including the United Nations Organization and the officer commanding the international police force, concerning (a) the uniform to be worn by a group of Canadian servicemen about to join the international police force; (b) the flag such group would fly?
Answer by: Mr. Cardin, Parliamentary Assistant, for the Secretary of State for External Affairs:
The answer to both these questions is "No". We have been informed that during the discussions last November, between the Secretary General of the United Nations and the government of Egypt, reference was made to the similarity in the uniform worn by Canadian troops to that worn by British forces, as a possible source of misunderstanding on the part of the Egyptian public. There were no representations, however, that Canadian troops participating in the United Nations emergency force would wear anything but their own uniforms together with the distinctive arm bands and headgear that were to be worn by all members of UNEF. Also, on the question of flags, there have been no representations to the Canadian government by or on behalf of the government of Egypt. The force as a whole, of course, operates under the United Nations flag, which is flown at the various headquarters and camps. National flags are, however, also flown on appropriate occasions and regulations governing this practice are being formalized by the United Nations authorities.
